column1: Underlying Core Inflation with Multiple Regimes

The thesis titled Underlying Core Inflation with Multiple Regimes by Gabriel Rodriguez-Rondon introduces a novel methodology for estimating core inflation indicators by leveraging common factors across a wide array of price indices. The paper proposes two distinct types of core inflation indicators: one that incorporates multiple structural breaks and another based on Markov switching. The structural breaks approach is effective in eliminating revisions for past regimes but is limited to offline use  as real-time detection of breaks is not feasible. Conversely  the Markov switching approach is advantageous for real-time application  reducing revisions and serving as a robust core inflation indicator suitable for real-time monitoring and short-term monetary policy guidance. This approach also allows for estimating the probability of being in different inflationary regimes.

The effectiveness of these indicators is demonstrated using Canadian price data. The study compares the real-time performance of the Markov switching approach against a benchmark model without regime-switching  focusing on their ability to forecast headline inflation and minimize revisions. The findings indicate that the Markov switching model offers superior predictive accuracy and significantly reduces revisions during periods of substantial inflation changes. This suggests that accounting for time-varying factors and parameters enhances the accuracy of inflation signals and reduces data requirements  particularly following sudden economic shifts.

The paper acknowledges the challenges associated with core inflation indicators built using factor models  such as historical estimate revisions and debates over the number of factors to extract. Despite criticisms  the factor model-based approach has been bolstered by typically negligible revisions in the past. However  recent inflation surges have made these revisions more concerning  prompting some central banks to reconsider their use. The paper addresses these challenges by modernizing the factor-based approach with new econometric procedures  proposing indicators that account for time-varying dynamics and multiple inflation regimes.

The proposed indicators effectively eliminate or reduce historical revisions while retaining desirable features of core inflation indicators. The Markov-switching model  in particular  proves useful in real-time applications. Empirical application using Canadian price data supports the advantages of these indicators  with the Markov-switching approach demonstrating superior predictive accuracy and significantly reducing revisions during major inflation changes. This is particularly relevant for Canada  where the indicators address issues with the Bank of Canada's CPI-Common concerning revisions. The findings suggest that the CPI-Common with Markov switching  termed CPI-Common-MS  outperforms the basic CPI-Common in capturing inflation dynamics during significant inflation fluctuations  whether inflation is rising sharply or stabilizing. This effectiveness may stem from including data from a past high-inflation period in Canada  specifically between January 1990 and late 1991  prior to the Bank's adoption of inflation targeting.
